paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses which expensive function evaluation to perform next. Expected Improvement favors evaluations with promising potential to improve the best result, while information-based methods seek to reduce uncertainty about the optimum. These objectives are often treated as fundamentally different ways to guide the search.

The paper introduces Variational Entropy Search, a theoretical framework that connects these approaches. It shows that Expected Improvement can be understood as a variational inference approximation to Max-value Entropy Search. This interpretation makes the relationship mathematically explicit: a familiar improvement-based rule can arise as an approximation within an information-based formulation.

The authors use this connection to develop VES-Gamma, an acquisition function intended to combine strengths of both methods. Evaluations cover synthetic and real-world benchmarks in low and high dimensions. VES-Gamma is competitive with state-of-the-art acquisition functions and often outperforms Expected Improvement and Max-value Entropy Search. The contribution therefore includes both a reinterpretation of existing methods and an empirically useful search rule derived from that reinterpretation.
icml-2025-a-unified-framework-for-entrop.tldr: Variational Entropy Search connects Expected Improvement to information-based Bayesian optimization and yields a competitive acquisition function.

paragraphs: Optimization constrained by partial differential equations can require repeated, costly numerical calculations. Neural operators can act as faster substitutes, but gradient-based optimization needs accurate derivatives as well as accurate predictions. Errors in either can push optimization off course, while collecting useful training data can itself be inefficient.

The proposed framework addresses these issues together. It trains neural operators using data from the full steps of traditional optimization algorithms, with training tailored to their eventual optimization role. A Virtual-Fourier layer strengthens derivative learning. A hybrid optimization procedure then combines the learned operator with numerical solvers, providing regularization during the search.

The experiments report effective learning of both operators and their derivatives, alongside robust convergence of the hybrid procedure. These findings matter because a surrogate that predicts well is not automatically sufficient for reliable gradient-based decisions. The paper makes derivative quality, optimization-relevant training data, and continued numerical-solver involvement central parts of the acceleration strategy.
icml-2025-accelerating-pde-constrained-o.tldr: Optimization-oriented training, improved derivative learning, and numerical-solver support make neural operators more useful for accelerating PDE-constrained optimization.

paragraphs: In a multi-agent linear bandit problem, several agents learn which actions produce good outcomes. Sharing observations can make learning more efficient, but another agent’s data may reflect different underlying parameters. Collaboration must therefore account for whether additional evidence improves an estimate or pulls it toward an inappropriate value.

The paper formalizes this tension as a trade-off between estimation bias and uncertainty. That result provides the foundation for Bandit Adaptive Sample Sharing, or BASS. Unlike most existing approaches discussed in the abstract, the method does not require assumptions about structural relationships among agents’ bandit parameters. Its collaboration strategy is grounded in the estimation trade-off instead.

Theoretical analysis and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support BASS’s efficiency relative to current state-of-the-art methods. The authors also show that when agents’ parameters have a cluster structure, the algorithm accurately recovers those clusters. This conditional finding is useful: the method can exploit such organization when present without requiring it as a starting assumption.
icml-2025-adaptive-sample-sharing-for-mu.tldr: BASS adapts data sharing between bandit agents by balancing estimation bias and uncertainty without assuming a parameter structure.

paragraphs: Learning several reinforcement-learning tasks together becomes difficult when tasks differ in complexity and in the rewards they produce. The numerical scale of rewards is therefore part of the training problem, alongside learning the behaviors themselves. Adaptive Reward Scaling, or ARS, addresses these differences by changing reward magnitudes during learning.

ARS uses reward history to adjust scaling and balance reward distributions across tasks. It pairs this strategy with periodic network resets, which the authors describe as reducing overfitting and supporting robust convergence. The two components address related training difficulties: scaling balances the reward signals, while resetting helps counter overfitting in the network.

On the Meta-World benchmark, ARS significantly outperforms the evaluated baseline methods. The reported improvements include stronger performance on challenging tasks while preserving overall learning efficiency. These results support the usefulness of combining adaptive reward treatment with resets for multi-task training. The broader promise is more scalable learning across diverse tasks, with the concrete empirical evidence supplied by the Meta-World evaluations.
icml-2025-ars-adaptive-reward-scaling-fo.tldr: ARS combines history-based reward scaling and periodic network resets to improve multi-task reinforcement learning on Meta-World.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning represents the variability of future returns rather than only their average. This can capture environmental randomness, but a full return distribution is infinite-dimensional. The paper examines how such information can support provably efficient learning when value functions are approximated, working in finite episodic Markov decision processes.

The authors introduce Bellman unbiasedness as a requirement for distributional updates that are exactly learnable online and provably efficient. Their theoretical analysis identifies moment functionals as the only statistical functionals that exactly capture the relevant information under this framework. The significance is about the representation needed for these exact updates, rather than a blanket dismissal of other distributional representations.

The paper also proposes SF-LSVI and proves a tight regret bound of Õ(d_E H^(3/2) √K), where H is the horizon, K the number of episodes, and d_E the function class’s eluder dimension. This connects learning efficiency to episode length and function-class complexity, providing a concrete theoretical foundation for distributional learning in the stated setting.
icml-2025-bellman-unbiasedness-toward-pr.tldr: Bellman unbiasedness characterizes exact distributional updates and supports a reinforcement-learning algorithm with a tight regret guarantee.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links two optimization problems: an upper-level choice must respect an optimal solution to a lower-level problem. This becomes especially expensive when functions are noisy, constrained, or accessible only through evaluations. Repeatedly solving the lower problem consumes samples, while relying on an estimated solution risks using one that is suboptimal.

BILBO tackles both levels simultaneously through Bayesian optimization. It samples within trusted sets constructed from confidence bounds, which bound lower-level suboptimality. Each iteration makes only one function query. The query-selection strategy accounts for uncertainty in estimated lower-level solutions and can conditionally redirect the query to encourage exploration of the lower-level objective.

This design makes deciding what to evaluate part of the coupled optimization procedure, reducing dependence on repeated lower-level searches. The authors prove a sublinear regret bound for commonly used kernels and evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world problems. The theoretical result supplies a qualified performance guarantee, while the experiments examine the algorithm’s behavior on concrete bilevel tasks.
icml-2025-bilbo-bilevel-bayesian-optimiz.tldr: BILBO jointly optimizes both levels of a black-box bilevel problem using confidence-based trusted sets and one function query per iteration.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers change their step sizes using gradient information. When stochastic gradients have heavy-tailed noise, unusually large disturbances can make reliable convergence difficult. The paper studies high-probability guarantees, which concern how confidently an optimizer’s convergence can be bounded rather than only its average behavior.

The authors prove that AdaGrad and Adam, including delayed versions, can have poor high-probability convergence under heavy-tailed noise. They then derive improved guarantees for clipped AdaGrad-Norm and Adam-Norm, with and without delay, in smooth convex and non-convex stochastic optimization. The bounds have polylogarithmic dependence on the confidence level. They also extend results to AdaGrad and Adam with delayed step sizes.

Empirical evaluations favor clipped versions when handling heavy-tailed noise. Together, the theory and experiments explain why adaptive step sizes alone may leave an optimizer vulnerable to extreme gradient disturbances, and why clipping can help. The negative result establishes that poor behavior is possible in the studied setting; it does not say every use of unclipped Adam or AdaGrad must fail.
icml-2025-clipping-improves-adam-norm-an.tldr: Gradient clipping improves high-probability convergence guarantees for adaptive optimizers facing heavy-tailed gradient noise.

paragraphs: Copilot Arena evaluates coding models inside developers’ working environments by collecting preferences between pairs of suggestions. This makes the evaluation reflect coding assistance as people encounter it during work. The platform includes an interface for comparing outputs, a sampling strategy that reduces experienced latency, and a prompting scheme for code completion.

The reported deployment served more than 4.5 million suggestions from 10 models and gathered over 11,000 pairwise judgments. Rankings from these judgments differ from rankings in existing evaluations. The authors attribute the difference to Copilot Arena’s particular distribution of data and tasks, highlighting that evaluation context can change the picture of model quality.

The preference analysis also finds consistency across programming languages but substantial variation across task categories. This suggests that what developers are trying to accomplish is a meaningful dimension of coding-assistant evaluation. By releasing the platform and data, the authors provide a basis for studying these human preferences and evaluating assistants in integrated development settings.
icml-2025-copilot-arena-a-platform-for-c.tldr: Copilot Arena gathers developer preferences during real coding work and reveals model rankings that differ from existing evaluations.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization can choose evaluations by considering how they affect several future decisions. This lookahead helps avoid shortsighted search, but becomes difficult as the number of input dimensions grows. Existing approaches often need substantial approximations or encounter scaling problems when reasoning over possible sequences of evaluations.

EARL-BO uses reinforcement learning to address the sequential decision problem underlying multi-step Bayesian optimization. An Attention-DeepSets encoder represents the current state of knowledge for the learning agent. The framework also includes a multi-task fine-tuning procedure that trains the encoder and reinforcement-learning component together through on-policy learning. The authors describe this as efficiently solving the sequential dynamic program in a near-optimal manner.

Evaluations on synthetic benchmark functions and hyperparameter-tuning problems show significantly better performance than the compared multi-step lookahead and high-dimensional Bayesian optimization methods. The approach matters because it makes representation learning and sequential decision-making part of the same optimization framework. Its reported gains support using a learned decision process to improve the scalability and quality of lookahead search.
icml-2025-earl-bo-reinforcement-learning.tldr: EARL-BO combines a learned knowledge encoder with reinforcement learning to improve multi-step Bayesian optimization in high dimensions.

paragraphs: Video prediction could help embodied systems anticipate how their surroundings will change. Existing video generators can simulate future states, but limited understanding can weaken predictions over multiple steps or in unfamiliar scenarios. The paper addresses these difficulties by combining visual-language understanding with video generation.

Reflection of Generation, or RoG, supplies intermediate reasoning strategies that connect pretrained vision-language and video-generation models. The authors also introduce EVA-Bench, which evaluates embodied world models across varied tasks using both familiar-distribution and out-of-distribution data. Their model, Embodied Video Anticipator, uses multistage training to generate high-fidelity frames and an autoregressive strategy to support longer video sequences.

Experiments demonstrate EVA’s effectiveness in downstream tasks including video generation and robotics. The contribution links a reasoning strategy, a dedicated evaluation benchmark, and a trained prediction model. This matters because useful embodied anticipation requires more than producing individual plausible frames: the work explicitly targets multi-step prediction and adaptation to longer sequences, while evaluating performance across both in-domain and unfamiliar settings.
icml-2025-empowering-world-models-with-r.tldr: RoG and EVA combine intermediate reasoning with video generation to improve embodied prediction, supported by a new benchmark.

paragraphs: Continual learning allows a language model to acquire knowledge as new tasks arrive. The paper focuses on online use, where revisiting information associated with previously learned tasks can create a problem. It calls this access or reuse information leakage and identifies both privacy concerns and practical deployment difficulties.

The proposed method organizes parameter-efficient fine-tuning blocks through feature distributions that characterize them. For each incoming instance, it compares that instance with the distributions and dynamically selects suitable blocks. This makes the characterization of each block central to deciding which learned adaptation should handle a particular input.

The authors propose this selection mechanism to avoid the identified leakage while retaining strong continual-learning performance. Extensive experiments support its effectiveness for language-model continual learning and suggest potential benefits for privacy and adaptability. The privacy claim is tied to avoiding the specific reuse problem described in the paper. The broader significance is an instance-dependent way to select existing adaptations as a model continues acquiring knowledge over time.
icml-2025-exploiting-presentative-featur.tldr: Feature-distribution-based selection of fine-tuning blocks supports continual language-model learning while addressing reuse of prior task information.

paragraphs: A language-model benchmark can give an inflated impression of generalization if its examples already appeared in pretraining. Kernel Divergence Score, or KDS, measures this contamination by examining how a model’s sample representations change when it is fine-tuned on the benchmark dataset.

The method constructs kernel similarity matrices from sample embeddings before and after fine-tuning, then measures the divergence between those matrices. Its guiding insight is that fine-tuning changes unseen samples more substantially than samples the model has already encountered. Looking at similarities between representations provides fine-grained information about these changes across the dataset.

In controlled contamination experiments, KDS has a near-perfect correlation with contamination levels and outperforms the evaluated baselines. Ablations examine design choices and support the importance of kernel-based information across diverse datasets and settings. These results establish strong empirical evidence for the score in the tested scenarios. They also explain why changes induced by fine-tuning can serve as a signal of prior benchmark exposure.
icml-2025-how-contaminated-is-your-bench.tldr: KDS estimates benchmark contamination from changes in embedding similarities before and after fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Dataset pruning reduces training and storage demands by removing redundant examples. However, identifying which examples to keep can itself require extensive training on the full dataset. The paper targets this overhead by scoring useful samples early enough for pruning to offer a more practical computational benefit.

Its DUAL score combines example difficulty with prediction uncertainty during early training. The method also uses sampling based on a Beta distribution that adapts to the pruning ratio. This additional component addresses severe accuracy losses when an extremely large fraction of the dataset is removed.

Experiments cover image classification, noisy labels, image corruption, and generalization across model architectures. On ImageNet-1k, pruning takes 66% of the time required by previous methods, with a reported state-of-the-art 60% test accuracy after removing 90% of the data. On CIFAR datasets, pruning time falls to 15% while retaining state-of-the-art performance. These findings connect early sample assessment with both lower selection costs and useful accuracy under aggressive pruning.
icml-2025-lightweight-dataset-pruning-wi.tldr: DUAL uses early example difficulty and prediction uncertainty to reduce dataset-pruning costs while preserving strong accuracy.

paragraphs: Decision trees and random forests are widely used for data represented in ordinary Euclidean spaces. This paper extends them to product manifolds, where a representation combines hyperbolic, hyperspherical, or Euclidean components. Such spaces can accommodate different curvatures within one representation while retaining a decomposition into simpler parts.

The method reformulates tree decisions in angular terms so that they respect the geometry of the representation. It preserves the algorithmic properties that make decision trees useful. When the manifold contains a single component, the approach reduces to Euclidean or hyperbolic counterparts, or provides a hyperspherical decision-tree algorithm, depending on that component’s curvature.

Across 57 classification, regression, and link-prediction tasks, the product random forests rank first on 29 tasks and among the top two on 41. These results support the practical value of adapting familiar tree methods to mixed-curvature representations. The contribution makes geometric embeddings usable with a straightforward predictive model family, extending the range of spaces in which trees and forests can operate.
icml-2025-mixed-curvature-decision-trees.tldr: An angular reformulation extends decision trees and random forests to mixed-curvature spaces, with strong results across 57 tasks.

paragraphs: Detection transformers spend substantial computation in their encoders, where image tokens can contain redundant information. Reducing the token count offers a route to efficiency, but token importance varies across representation levels and encoder blocks. A fixed sparsification strategy can therefore discard information that matters for detecting objects.

Dynamic DETR adjusts token density according to the importance distribution and sparsifies tokens at multiple levels. It aggregates nearby low-level tokens to maintain spatial structure, while using a holistic strategy for high-level tokens to retain broader context. Center-distance regularization aligns token distributions during this process, helping preserve consistent representations and object-specific patterns.

Experiments on established detection-transformer models show broad applicability and consistent improvements over the evaluated token-sparsification methods. The contribution is a structured way to reduce redundant computation while accounting for what different token levels represent. Its reported results support dynamic, level-sensitive aggregation as a useful approach to making detection transformers more efficient without losing the information that their detection process depends on.
icml-2025-not-all-tokens-matter-all-the-.tldr: Dynamic DETR adapts token aggregation across encoder levels to reduce redundancy while preserving spatial and object-specific information.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to produce models that work in unseen domains. A central difficulty is learning correlations specific to training domains that do not transfer. Gradient-based approaches can inadvertently reinforce these correlations when their updates favor a dominant direction or a small group of parameters.

GENIE introduces an optimizer guided by the One-Step Generalization Ratio, which measures each parameter’s contribution to loss reduction and assesses gradient alignment. A dynamically adjusted preconditioning factor equalizes these ratios. The intended effect is to prevent a few parameters from dominating optimization and encourage features that remain useful across domains.

The theoretical analysis shows balanced convergence contributions and gradient alignment, with higher One-Step Generalization Ratio while preserving SGD’s convergence rate. Experiments show improvements over existing optimizers and benefits when GENIE is incorporated into several domain-generalization and single-domain-generalization methods. These findings make parameter-level balance a concrete optimization mechanism for addressing transfer difficulties, with both theoretical support for its update behavior and empirical support for improved generalization.
icml-2025-one-step-generalization-ratio-.tldr: GENIE balances parameter contributions and gradient alignment to improve generalization to unseen domains.

paragraphs: Some training examples can harm a model’s performance, making their identification an important part of improving datasets. Influence functions assess how training data affect predictions, but their reliance on inverse-Hessian calculations creates substantial computational costs, especially for large neural networks.

The paper connects influence-function-based identification of harmful samples with detecting outliers among sample gradients. This yields a formulation that avoids Hessian calculations and offers another way to understand how an example affects learning. The key contribution is the relationship between a sample’s gradient behavior and its influence, providing a simpler route to analyzing detrimental training data.

The authors first test the approach’s underlying hypothesis on synthetic datasets. They then demonstrate detection of mislabeled examples in vision models and data selection that improves natural-language transformer performance. They also extend the method to finding influential samples for language-model fine-tuning. These applications show how the same gradient-based perspective can support several data-selection problems while addressing a major computational obstacle in influence analysis.
icml-2025-outlier-gradient-analysis-effi.tldr: Outlier gradient analysis connects harmful-sample detection to influence functions while avoiding expensive Hessian calculations.

paragraphs: Optimal transport seeks to move one distribution to another while minimizing transport cost. Neural methods based on a semi-dual formulation can produce spurious solutions: their learned maps fail to transfer the source distribution accurately. The paper investigates when this formulation recovers the intended transport map.

The authors establish a sufficient condition for its max-min solution to recover the true map. They also propose OTP for cases where that condition is not satisfied. OTP learns both a transport map and a transport plan, which describes the coupling between the distributions. Under stated sharp assumptions on the distributions, they prove that it avoids spurious solutions and solves the transport problem correctly.

Experiments show recovery of optimal maps in cases where existing methods fail, along with improvements over current transport-based image-translation models. OTP can also learn stochastic transport maps when deterministic optimal maps do not exist, including one-to-many tasks such as colorization. This extends the method’s relevance to problems where a single fixed output for each input cannot express the required transport.
icml-2025-overcoming-spurious-solutions-.tldr: OTP learns transport maps and plans to address spurious neural optimal-transport solutions, with guarantees under distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback uses preferences to help align behavior with human goals. The paper identifies a likelihood-estimation problem in existing approaches: they can treat observed trajectories as if an optimal policy generated them. When that interpretation is inaccurate, it can undermine the learning process.

Policy-labeled Preference Learning, or PPL, addresses the mismatch within the Direct Preference Optimization framework. It models preferences using regret, incorporating the efficiency of the policies that produced the trajectories. The authors also derive a contrastive KL regularization term from regret-based principles to strengthen sequential contrastive learning. Both changes connect preference learning more directly to the behavior of the executed policies.

Experiments in high-dimensional continuous-control environments show significant improvements in offline reinforcement learning from human feedback, along with effectiveness in online settings. The findings support accounting for policy quality when interpreting trajectory preferences. The paper’s contribution is therefore both a revised preference model and an accompanying regularizer, evaluated in control tasks where behavior unfolds over sequences of actions.
icml-2025-policy-labeled-preference-lear.tldr: PPL models preferences through policy regret to correct likelihood mismatches and improve feedback-based learning in continuous control.

paragraphs: Replacing a foundation model can make task-specific adaptation costly because the new model may need to be fine-tuned again. Existing inference-time tuning approaches reuse adaptation by combining outputs from the new model, the old model, and its fine-tuned version. Running those additional models creates an inference cost.

Portable Reward Tuning reformulates fine-tuning as reward maximization with Kullback-Leibler regularization. It explicitly trains a reward model using the same loss as fine-tuning, instead of updating the foundation model’s parameters. At inference time, that reward model can guide a foundation model through the reward-maximization formulation. Portability requires the models to share the same vocabulary or label set.

Experiments involving vision and language models find accuracy comparable to existing inference-time tuning while using less inference computation. The significance is that task adaptation is represented in a reusable reward model, reducing dependence on repeatedly running both an old base model and its tuned counterpart. The shared-vocabulary or shared-label condition defines the stated scope of that reuse.
icml-2025-portable-reward-tuning-towards.tldr: Portable Reward Tuning stores task adaptation in a reward model reusable across foundation models with matching vocabularies or labels.

paragraphs: Low-bit quantization can reduce the size and computational demands of state space models, but these models are sensitive to quantization errors. Deployment also calls for different weight and activation precisions across platforms. Quamba2 supports Mamba and Mamba2 with W8A8, W4A8, and W4A16 configurations, covering several such requirements.

The framework sorts and clusters the recurrence input x offline for 8-bit quantization, and applies quantization by state groups to B and C. It also rearranges weights offline according to the clustering order so that the rearrangement preserves the SSM’s computation. These coordinated changes address quantization within the recurrence rather than treating every internal quantity identically.

Experiments report that Quamba2-8B outperforms several state-of-the-art SSM quantization methods. The reported outcomes include 1.3× faster pre-filling, 3× faster generation, and a fourfold memory reduction, with an average accuracy drop of 1.6%. These measurements demonstrate a practical efficiency–accuracy trade-off in the evaluated setting, while the supported precision configurations broaden the framework’s deployment applicability.
icml-2025-quamba2-a-robust-and-scalable-.tldr: Quamba2 supports multiple low-bit Mamba configurations using coordinated recurrence quantization, delivering reported speed and memory gains.

paragraphs: Neural-network verification needs bounds that are both computationally manageable and sufficiently tight. Linear bound propagation scales to large networks, but can lose precision when relationships among neurons matter. Semidefinite programming captures those relationships more naturally, although its cubic computational complexity limits the size of models it can handle.

SDP-CROWN introduces a linear bound derived from semidefinite-programming principles. It captures coupling among neurons based on the ℓ2 norm while adding just one parameter per layer. Because the bound fits into linear bound-propagation pipelines, the framework aims to retain their scalability while incorporating information that traditional per-neuron bounds miss.

The authors prove that the new bound can be up to √n times tighter than traditional per-neuron bounds. Integrated into α-CROWN, it improves verification on evaluated models containing up to 65,000 neurons and 2.47 million parameters, with tightness approaching more expensive SDP methods. The theoretical improvement is a possible factor, while the experiments establish practical gains for the tested integration and models.
icml-2025-sdp-crown-efficient-bound-prop.tldr: SDP-CROWN incorporates neuron coupling into scalable bound propagation, improving verification tightness with one additional parameter per layer.

paragraphs: CAD sketches contain both continuous geometric parameters and discrete labels identifying primitive types. Generating them requires handling these different kinds of variables together. SketchDNN uses a unified diffusion process to model both, addressing the mixed structure of sketch data within a single generative formulation.

Its central mechanism is Gaussian-Softmax diffusion. Gaussian noise perturbs logits, and a softmax transformation turns them into class probabilities. This allows discrete labels to pass through blended representations during diffusion. The formulation addresses two challenges: different primitive types have heterogeneous parameterizations, and the ordering of primitives should not determine the sketch they represent.

On SketchGraphs, the reported Fréchet Inception Distance improves from 16.04 to 7.80, while negative log-likelihood falls from 84.8 to 81.33. The authors report a new state of the art in CAD sketch generation on that dataset. These results support jointly modeling discrete and continuous structure, with the diffusion formulation explicitly accommodating the parameter diversity and permutation invariance of CAD primitives.
icml-2025-sketchdnn-joint-continuous-dis.tldr: SketchDNN jointly diffuses continuous geometry and discrete primitive labels, improving CAD sketch generation on SketchGraphs.

paragraphs: Tabular models are often studied in closed environments, even though real deployments can involve changes in both data distributions and available features. This paper focuses on feature shifts, a challenge that has received less attention than distribution shifts. It introduces TabFSBench to make their effects a systematic target of evaluation.

The benchmark examines four feature-shift scenarios across four categories of tabular models and multiple datasets. It also evaluates large language models and tabular language models. This breadth allows the study to compare how different model families behave when the feature setting changes, rather than judging them only under their original closed-environment conditions.

The study reports that most tabular models have limited applicability under feature shifts. It also observes a linear relationship between the importance of the shifted feature set and performance degradation, plus a correlation between closed-environment and feature-shift performance. These are empirical relationships from the benchmark. They help organize questions about which shifts are damaging and how existing evaluations relate to performance in changing environments.
icml-2025-tabfsbench-tabular-benchmark-f.tldr: TabFSBench systematically evaluates tabular feature shifts and finds widespread model difficulties alongside relationships involving feature importance and baseline performance.

paragraphs: Model merging combines task-specific experts into one model, but their parameters can interfere and degrade performance. Addressing this without additional training data or test-time computation is difficult. WUDI-Merging uses information in task vectors to guide how that interference is resolved.

The theoretical starting point is that a linear layer’s task vectors form an approximate linear subspace for its corresponding input. The authors use this relationship to guide interference minimization. Their resulting merging method is described as eliminating interference without additional data or rescaling coefficients, with low computational requirements. The approximate nature of the subspace relationship is part of the underlying theoretical claim.

Across the evaluated vision and language benchmarks, WUDI-Merging achieves reported state-of-the-art results for data-free merging. The abstract reports an average 10.9% improvement over baseline methods and a 3.3% improvement over mainstream test-time adaptation approaches. These findings support task vectors as useful guidance for combining experts while avoiding the additional data and computation associated with other adaptation strategies.
icml-2025-whoever-started-the-interferen.tldr: WUDI-Merging uses task-vector geometry to address interference when combining expert models without additional data or rescaling coefficients.
